text:
nina roberts: quick sync: after the modularization RFC i sketched a small alternative called "adapter canalization" — basically a thin adapter layer that funnels hotpath requests through stable runtime contracts. doc: https://docs.internal/rfcs/adapter-canalization

diego marcos: naming aside, what problem does canalization solve vs full service split?

nina roberts: intent is to reduce blast radius of service fission. instead of splitting service into many small services, we insert adapters that decouple implementations while keeping runtime placement the same. cheaper rollbacks, smaller PRs.

kevin wu: what about latency on the hotpath? even small increases matter.

nina roberts: agreed. our micro-bench spike shows ~0.5ms median per adapter using shared-process adapters (no RPC). net added p50 ~0.2ms because other savings appear (simpler code paths). details in doc.

anya ivanova: how do we avoid adapter proliferation? i worry teams will create adapters for everything and we'll end up with the same maintenance surface but more indirection.

nina roberts: governance rules proposed: 1) adapter only when it buys decoupling impossible with internal module boundaries; 2) must be approved by owning product + infra; 3) each adapter gets a retention TTL and an owner tag.

diego marcos: enforcement? auto-expiry tickets?

kevin wu: we can add a lint that flags adapters without owner or TTL in the manifest. fails CI for new adapters.

anya ivanova: ok, what about testing matrix? if adapters are small, unit tests per-adapter are cheap, but integration multiplies.

nina roberts: proposal: contract-driven tests. each adapter publishes a JSON schema and a small contract test harness. CI categories: quick unit tests (patch), contract smoke (on PR), full integration (nightly or selective). use tags to gate heavy suites.

kevin wu: example contract snippet?

nina roberts: pasted simple schema in doc, e.g.:

```json
{"request": {"type": "object", "props": {"session_id": {"type": "string"}}}, "response": {"type": "object", "props": {"token_count": {"type": "integer"}}}}
```

kevin wu: nice. how do we handle versioning? adapters change over time.

nina roberts: semver for contract-v + runtime fallback rules. adapters annotate responses with `X-Contract-V` and runtime router picks compatible adapters or falls back to legacy path. we'll emit metrics for any fallback.

anya ivanova: observability: tracing, token/cost attribution, latency percentiles per-contract?

nina roberts: yes — adapters propagate trace context, add `contract_id` tag, and we add per-contract dashboards in console. also alert on contract error-rate > 0.5% for 5m.

diego marcos: rollout plan? who's owning the first wave?

nina roberts: suggested phase-0: session-coordinator adapter (low risk, high coupling), then kv-cache gateway. timeline 8 weeks for phase-0. i'll draft tickets for owners and per-adapter checklists: feature-flag, perf bench, canary, ramp, remove legacy.

kevin wu: CI side: implement adapter lint + selective-integration gating. infra can help with a reservable canary window.

ops-bot: Note: canary window requests accepted. Add your team to the canary calendar at https://infra.internal/canary-calendar

anya ivanova: one last risk: debugging cognitive load. new layer means new mental model for oncall. ops runbook?

nina roberts: adding an ops runbook section to the doc with quick triage steps (identify contract_id, check fallback metrics, revert feature flag). i'll also run a 45min training for oncall next sprint.

diego marcos: sounds pragmatic. small, reversible changes are better than a risky big split. +1 to starting with session-coordinator.

kevin wu: i'll volunteer to pair on the perf tuning and the lint rules.

nina roberts: thanks both. i'll post the RFC update and create the phase-0 ticket board. meeting to finalize owners Wed 10am.

ops-bot: Document updated by nina roberts (adapter-canalization) - view: https://docs.internal/rfcs/adapter-canalization (rev2)

anya ivanova: thanks, look forward to the sync.
